note.specFocus: The meaning and celebration of the two most important festivals in the Christian calendar.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.1 Christmas and Easter
Christmas and Easter are the two most widely recognised Christian festivals, celebrating the incarnation and the resurrection respectively.
Christmas
• Celebrates the birth of Jesus, the incarnation of God as a human being, central to the Christmas story in Luke 2 and Matthew 1–2.
• Celebrated through Advent (a season of preparation), nativity plays, carol services and, for many, Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve.
Easter
• Celebrates Jesus' resurrection from the dead, which St Paul calls the very foundation of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14).
• Preceded by Lent (40 days of fasting, prayer and reflection) and Holy Week — Maundy Thursday (the Last Supper), Good Friday (the crucifixion) and Holy Saturday — before Easter Sunday celebrations, often including the lighting of the Paschal (Easter) candle and the greeting "Christ is risen! He is risen indeed!"
Which is more important?
• Theologically, many Christians consider Easter the more significant festival, since the resurrection, not the birth narrative alone, is presented in the New Testament as proof that Jesus overcame sin and death.
• Christmas, however, remains hugely popular and widely celebrated, though often criticised by Christians for becoming commercialised and losing its religious focus in wider secular culture.
Exam link: "Discuss" questions often ask you to weigh the cultural/commercial side of Christmas against its continuing religious meaning for practising Christians — use both sides.

evidence: Holy Week: Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Easter Sunday
questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Many Christians attend a special Easter Sunday service celebrating Jesus' resurrection, often including joyful hymns, the lighting of the Paschal (Easter) candle and the greeting "Christ is risen! He is risen indeed!"

2. The period of Lent, forty days of fasting, prayer and reflection leading up to Easter, and Holy Week, including Maundy Thursday (the Last Supper), Good Friday (the crucifixion) and Holy Saturday, prepare Christians spiritually to fully celebrate Easter Sunday.
questions.question: Outline two ways in which Christians celebrate Easter.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus from the dead, which St Paul describes as the very foundation of Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14), since without the resurrection Christians believe their faith would be meaningless.

Second, The resurrection is understood as proof that Jesus overcame sin and death, giving Christians hope and assurance of their own resurrection and eternal life, which is a central promise of the Christian faith.

Finally, Unlike Christmas, which celebrates Jesus' birth, Easter marks the completion of Jesus' saving work; this is why Holy Week and Easter are given such prominence in the Church calendar, with many churches treating Easter, not Christmas, as the most theologically significant festival.
questions.question: Explain why Easter is the most important festival for Christians.

questions.examTip: For a 10-mark discussion, analyse different aspects of the Christian issue and how they interrelate. Finish with a reasoned conclusion; do not just list advantages and disadvantages.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: In many countries, Christmas has become heavily commercialised, with an emphasis on gift-giving, decorations and parties that have little connection to the Christian story of Jesus' birth, which some Christians feel has overshadowed the festival's original meaning.

A second consideration is: Surveys suggest that a large proportion of people who celebrate Christmas do not attend a religious service or reflect on the incarnation, focusing instead on family traditions that are largely secular in practice.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Many Christians would respond that churches remain full for events such as Midnight Mass and carol services, and that for believers, Christmas retains its core meaning as a celebration of the incarnation, God becoming human in Jesus, regardless of the surrounding secular culture.

A further consideration is: Some Christians also see opportunities within the wider cultural celebration of Christmas, such as carol singing, nativity plays and charitable giving, as ways the Christian message can still reach people who might not otherwise engage with church.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: whether Christmas has "lost" its meaning may depend on whether the focus is on wider secular culture, where commercial elements dominate, or on practising Christians and churches, for whom the incarnation remains central. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.
questions.question: Discuss whether Christmas has lost its religious meaning.

evidence: resurrection and the risk of commercial celebration

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of Incarnation, Holy Week, crucifixion, resurrection and the risk of commercial celebration and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
